title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language

Title:Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 55% of 15K anonymous ICML 2020 reviews that were never made public, and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.

report.summary: A new arXiv study finds frontier models can identify whether text was written by AI or a human—and often pinpoint the exact author—from a single zero-shot prompt.
report.background: For years, AI-text detection relied on trained classifiers that scored patterns like perplexity and burstiness, while authorship attribution used forensic stylometry requiring known writing samples. Both approaches struggled with short texts, false positives, and adversaries who paraphrased. The new paper argues frontier LLMs change the game because they are pretrained on massive public writing, including reviews, forum posts, and social media. That exposure lets a general-purpose model recognize stylistic fingerprints without task-specific training, web search, or candidate lists. The result challenges assumptions behind anonymous peer review, pseudonymous online accounts, and whistleblower protections, and it raises questions about whether public writing is effectively a biometric identifier. It also puts pressure on platforms and researchers to develop privacy-preserving writing tools and better anonymity defenses before attribution becomes routine.
key_points: The paper tests a zero-shot prompt that asks a model 'who wrote this?' without web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples. Models answer at three levels: AI or human, which AI lab if machine-generated, and often the exact human author. The latest frontier models reportedly match dedicated detectors such as Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language.

Accuracy is strikingly high in the reported experiments. Opus 5.5 identifies the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models. Fable 5.2 names the author of 55% of 15,000 anonymous ICML 2020 reviews that were never publicly released, and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors with more than 500 posts in a year.

The mechanism is exposure, not magic. Attribution accuracy depends on how much of an author's writing appeared in pretraining data and on how much reasoning effort the model spends. Simply asking a model how familiar it is with a person predicts whether it can identify that person's writing, suggesting models carry implicit style profiles from public text.

Defenses are limited. The authors warn that anyone who has published enough writing online faces a greater anonymity risk than commonly assumed. Because the attack needs only one text and a simple prompt, it is cheap and scalable, making traditional safeguards such as removing names or using pseudonyms insufficient on their own.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper shifts detection from specialized classifiers to general-purpose model capabilities, blurring lines between content moderation, forensic attribution, and privacy invasion. Developers building anonymous or pseudonymous products must assume that public writing can fingerprint users; they should audit pretraining leakage, offer paraphrasing or style-scrubbing tools, and design data-minimization defaults. Platforms and peer-review systems may need stricter anonymity protocols, such as style-preserving transformations or restricted text release. For regular users, the risk is concentrated among people with large public writing footprints—journalists, whistleblowers, activists, and prolific reviewers—not everyone. Still, the finding normalizes a world where a single post can be traced, so users should treat pseudonymity as fragile and demand clearer consent and deletion controls.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Pangram (the trained detector benchmarked in the paper), open-source stylometry toolkits such as stylo in R and JGAAP, and privacy-oriented text anonymization projects like Textwash. Researchers can monitor the paper's arXiv page for code and data links; developers can test adversarial paraphrasing and style-transfer pipelines against attribution prompts. Also watch platform-level anonymity features and emerging 'unlearning' or data-deletion tools that reduce pretraining exposure.
